factual_and_methodological.summary: Core claims were checked against Bank of Israel and IMF historical evidence. Bank of Israel corroborates 1984 inflation around 445–450%, fiscal/expenditure and subsidy adjustment, wage restraint coordinated with Histadrut, devaluation and exchange-rate stabilization, and the restriction on direct central-bank credit to government. The report correctly treats the program as a synchronized package and avoids identifying a clean independent causal effect for any single instrument.

editorial_publication_readiness.opening: Direct analytical opening identifies the synchronized-anchor mechanism without generic summary scaffolding.
editorial_publication_readiness.headings: Headings name initial conditions, coordinated design, transmission, observed inflation break, distribution, implementation, durability and transfer limits.
editorial_publication_readiness.language_localization: EN and PT-BR are natural and semantically equivalent; specialist terms are explained in context.
editorial_publication_readiness.repetition: No blocking repetition; the multi-anchor caveat is reused only where it changes causal interpretation or transferability.
editorial_publication_readiness.cohesion: The argument moves from indexed inflation through package design and transmission to outcomes, distribution, political economy, adaptation and comparative limits.
editorial_publication_readiness.template_meta_qa: No prompt, QA-process or template leakage detected.

contextual_depth.summary: Indexation, centralized wage bargaining, fiscal financing, exchange-rate institutions and later inflation-targeting adaptation are integrated into the causal mechanism.

visual_evidence_readiness.signature: Three analytical tables, one inflation bar chart and one causal flow; EN/PT-BR are semantically parallel.
visual_evidence_readiness.limitations: The first chart bar intentionally encodes 15 as a lower bound for a source statement of more than 15%; the caption and prose disclose this explicitly. Simultaneous instruments prevent component-level causal attribution.

contrary_evidence: Bank of Israel research indicates the exchange-rate anchor was important for the initial disinflation but did not by itself drive inflation progressively lower afterward; later exchange-rate flexibility and inflation targeting mattered.
The simultaneous fiscal, monetary, exchange-rate and incomes-policy interventions prevent clean attribution of the observed inflation decline to any one instrument.
Distributional costs from wage restraint, subsidy changes and expenditure cuts mean rapid disinflation cannot be treated as a one-dimensional welfare result.
limitations: Historical percentage descriptions of the initial devaluation vary with measurement convention; the report appropriately emphasizes the institutional sequence rather than a disputed percentage.
The chart's H1 1985 value is a disclosed lower-bound visualization, not an exact point estimate.
Transferability depends on indexation structure, fiscal consistency, bargaining institutions and administrative capacity.
notes: New policy-case publication candidate. Primary Bank of Israel evidence supports the central mechanism and the report preserves attribution limits; no public bundle for this ID was present at the reviewed content state.

en.title: Israel's 1985 stabilization: why several nominal anchors had to move together
en.deck: The July 1985 program combined fiscal correction, tight money, exchange-rate stabilization and a negotiated wage-price framework to interrupt an inflation process embedded in several indexed institutions at once.
en.regime: Synchronized fiscal, monetary, exchange-rate and incomes-policy stabilization after inflation became embedded in several indexed institutions
en.key_risk: Reducing the episode to one anchor obscures both the fiscal consistency required for the initial break and the later need to adapt the exchange-rate regime.
